title: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)
hook: RLHF works but is fiddly: a separate reward model and a finicky RL loop. DPO reaches the same goal with one simple loss — and became a popular default.
key_points: Aligns a model directly on preference pairs with a single classification-style loss.
No separate reward model and no reinforcement-learning loop to tune.
Derived to optimize the same objective RLHF targets, but in closed form.
More stable and simpler to run, while matching RLHF-level quality.
content_html: Rafael Rafailov, Archit Sharma, and colleagues at Stanford asked whether you really need reinforcement learning to align a model to human preferences. DPO shows you don't. They rederive the RLHF objective so the language model itself implicitly acts as the reward model, collapsing the whole pipeline into a single supervised loss over preference pairs — simpler, more stable, and competitive in quality.
extra_html:
How it works

RLHF first fits a reward model to preference data, then runs RL to maximize that reward with a penalty for drifting from the reference model. DPO observes that this objective has a closed-form relationship between the optimal policy and the reward, so the reward can be expressed in terms of the policy itself. Substituting that in turns the problem into a simple binary classification loss: increase the model's relative likelihood of the preferred response over the rejected one in each pair, weighted against a frozen reference. No reward model, no sampling, no RL loop.

Why it matters

The RL stage of RLHF is the hardest part to get working — it needs careful tuning and is sensitive to instability. DPO removes that stage entirely while targeting the same goal, so teams can align models with familiar supervised training. Because it is easier to run and reproduces RLHF-level results, it became a widely used default for preference alignment.

related.title: InstructGPT: Aligning LMs with Human Feedback (RLHF)
related.hook: A smaller model people actually like beats a bigger one they don't. InstructGPT used human preferences to make a model follow instructions — the recipe behind ChatGPT.

related.title: PPO: Proximal Policy Optimization
related.hook: Reinforcement learning is notoriously unstable. PPO's fix is simple: never let a single update move the policy too far. That restraint made it the field's workhorse.
